p: Tuesday, November 10, 9:20 in the morning, and the endorsement took Abby forty seconds to write. One dual to the practice area and back, steep turns, two stalls, a simulated engine failure over a sugar beet field east of Bennett that Jordan picked early and flew to like she'd been told where it was. On the ramp Abby uncapped the green pen and wrote it standing up, using the wing as a desk.
Practice area. Alone. Still under the shelf, still back by noon, still your card. She capped the pen. Now the part where you leave.
Cross-country. You go somewhere, you land, you come home. Thursday at four. Bring the chart, the plotter, and a pencil you don't love.

She'd bought the plotter the Saturday before, at the pilot shop by the FBO. Clear plastic, nine dollars, a ruler on one edge and a half moon of degrees in the middle. The man behind the counter had tried to sell her a forty dollar one with a light in it. She'd said her instructor said not the fancy one, and he'd nodded like he'd heard that before, which he probably had.

The other tool came out of Biscuit's door pocket. She'd found it in April, under the fuel tester and a parking receipt from 2019, and put it back without knowing what it was. Now she knew. An E6B flight computer, the aluminum kind, a slide rule on one side and a clear window over a sliding grid on the other, with D. REYES scratched on the back in capitals somebody had made with a key. On the wind side, in the middle of the frosted window, there was a pencil dot. A little circle around it. His last wind, whatever it had been.
She didn't erase it. She worked her first practice problem in the margin, around it.
That night Walt texted. Walt didn't text.
A text from Walt Herrera. Seven and a half months. Cross-country is where students stall. Weather, scheduling, nerves. I'd like to be wrong about this one.
She read it twice and decided it was the nicest thing he'd ever said to her, which told her something about Walt, and maybe about her.

Everything so far has been within sight of the tower. Today you learn to leave, and the regulations get specific the minute you do. 61.93 says a student pilot needs its training and endorsements before a solo cross-country, or any flight more than 25 nautical miles from the airport where it started, or any solo landing somewhere other than where you took off. Your practice area endorsement doesn't stretch to cover that. This one is its own animal.

Here's what 61.93 wants. First, training from me on a list in paragraph (e): charts with pilotage and dead reckoning and the magnetic compass, performance charts, weather reports and forecasts including estimating visibility in flight, emergency procedures, area departures and arrivals and pattern entries, collision avoidance, wake turbulence, and windshear, the terrain where you'll fly, the equipment in this airplane, radios for navigation and talking, short and soft field and crosswind takeoffs and landings, best angle and best rate climbs, and flying by instruments. Second, two endorsements. One goes in your logbook once, saying you've had the training and you're proficient to fly solo cross-country in a Cessna 172N. The other goes in for each cross-country flight, after I've reviewed your planning, naming the route and the airports and the date.

That second one has teeth on my side too. Paragraph (d) says I can't let you go unless I've checked your planning is correct, reviewed the current and forecast weather and decided the flight can be finished under VFR, decided you're proficient for it, and checked that your endorsements are current. Your solo endorsement is good for 90 calendar days, so the one from October 20 carries you into January. After that, another one.

Now the definitions, because the test likes the trap. In everyday language a cross-country is any flight that lands somewhere else. For the hours that count toward your private certificate, 61.1 says a cross-country has to include a landing at a point more than 50 nautical miles, straight line, from where you started. Greeley is 53.0 miles from Centennial, measured from airport to airport. That landing is what makes Sunday count.

61.109 says you need 5 hours of solo cross-country, and inside that, one long one: 150 nautical miles total distance, full-stop landings at three points, and one leg that's more than 50 nautical miles straight line between takeoff and landing. Centennial, Greeley, the Space Port, and home is 53.0, then 39.5, then 19.3. That's 111.8 point to point. It counts toward the 5 hours. It isn't the long one. With all the doglegs around the Bravo you'll fly about 154 miles, and I'm not going to stand in front of an examiner and argue that three airports a hundred and twelve miles apart make a 150 mile trip. The long one is a different day, and you're going to plan it yourself.

How the exam asks it. Know that a student needs an instructor's review and endorsement for each solo cross-country, and that private pilot cross-country time needs a landing more than 50 NM from the departure point.

Pilotage is navigating by looking out the window: you match what's on the chart to what's on the ground. It's the oldest method and the one you'll use for the rest of your life, even with a screen in the panel, because the screen can be wrong and the interstate can't.

The PHAK has good advice on checkpoints. Pick things that are prominent and can be confirmed by something else nearby: a town where a highway crosses a railroad, a reservoir, a big interchange. Better still, pick features that bracket your course, a highway on one side and a river on the other, so if you cross one of them you know which way you've drifted. Never trust one checkpoint by itself. If you miss one, hold your heading and look for the next one. And the line I want you to say out loud: if confused, hold the heading. Turning to go look for something is how people get lost.

Scale matters. On a sectional, one inch is about 8 statute miles, which is 6.86 nautical. Half an inch off your line is three and a half miles on the ground. The chart also only shows the roads that are easy to see from the air, and new ones show up before the chart catches up. Out east that means a gravel road that isn't on the chart and a paved one that is. Trust the paved one.

Watch for towers. Antennas out there come in groups with guy wires you can't see, and some of them are taller than you'd believe. The PHAK says don't get within 500 feet above the tallest one. Greeley's Chart Supplement entry lists oil drilling rigs up to 120 feet on and around the airport. Out there they move. The chart doesn't know where they are this week.
How the exam asks it. Expect a question on selecting checkpoints and one on sectional scale. "Hold the heading" is the PHAK's answer when you're unsure.

Dead reckoning is the other half. It's navigation by arithmetic: time, airspeed, distance, and direction, corrected for the wind, which gives you a heading to fly and a groundspeed. The heading gets you there and the groundspeed tells you when you should see each checkpoint. You fly both at once. Dead reckoning tells you where you ought to be. Pilotage tells you where you are. The difference between them tells you what the wind is really doing.

The wind triangle is how you solve it. Three arrows. Your heading and true airspeed. The wind's direction and speed. Add them and you get your track over the ground and your groundspeed. You can draw it with a protractor, which the PHAK walks you through and the test sometimes makes you do. You can solve it on the wind side of an E6B, which is the dot and the grid. Or you can solve it with two sines and a cosine, which is what I'll show you in the drill, because it never lies about which way to turn.

The working version. Wind angle is the wind direction minus your true course. The wind correction angle is the inverse sine of the wind speed times the sine of the wind angle, divided by true airspeed. A positive answer means turn right, into a wind from the right. Groundspeed is true airspeed times the cosine of the correction angle, minus wind speed times the cosine of the wind angle. A headwind makes that last part big. A tailwind makes it negative, so you add it.

Where the wind comes from matters. The winds aloft forecast, the FB, gives directions in degrees true, speed in knots, and temperature in Celsius. 3216-06 at 9,000 means from 320 true at 16 knots, minus 6. The plotter measures true courses against the chart's true north lines. So you solve the whole triangle in true and only then convert to magnetic. One more Denver thing: the Aviation Weather Handbook says wind forecasts aren't issued within 1,500 feet of a location's elevation, so the Denver line is blank at 3,000 and 6,000 and starts at 9,000. For a 7,500 foot cruise you use the 9,000 number and you remember it's an estimate.
How the exam asks it. FB winds are true. Sectional courses are true. Solve the wind triangle in true, then convert. That's where most heading questions are won or lost.

The plotter gives you a true course. Biscuit's compass doesn't know what true north is. Getting from one to the other is a chain, and the PHAK prints it in one line: true course, plus or minus the wind correction angle, gives true heading. True heading, plus or minus variation, gives magnetic heading. Magnetic heading, plus or minus deviation, gives compass heading.

Variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north where you are. The sectional shows it with dashed magenta lines called isogonic lines; the one with zero variation is the agonic line, and it runs well east of here, down through Wisconsin and Illinois and western Tennessee. West of it, magnetic north is east of true. NOAA's model puts Centennial at 7.4 degrees east this month, a hair less at the Space Port, and we round to 7. East is least, west is best: subtract east variation, add west. A true heading of 071 is a magnetic heading of 064.

Deviation is the airplane's own fault. The engine, the radios, the steel in the seat frames all bend the compass a little, differently on different headings. Somebody swung Biscuit's compass on a compass rose, recorded what it read at every 30 degrees, and wrote a card. It's taped under the compass. It says FOR a magnetic heading, STEER this on the compass. Between the numbers, interpolate in your head. Within a degree is fine.

The compass has errors you have to fly around, and the test asks. On east or west headings, accelerating makes it swing toward north and slowing down makes it swing toward south. ANDS. Turning toward north in the northern hemisphere, the card lags, so you roll out before it gets there; the PHAK's rule of thumb is 15 degrees plus half your latitude early, so here about 35. Turning toward south it leads, so you go a little past. Undershoot north, overshoot south. And the heading indicator, the gyro, drifts. Friction moves it, and the earth turning underneath it can move it up to 15 degrees an hour. Straight and level, steady speed, reset it to the compass, and do it again every fifteen minutes or so. When the compass is swinging, use the middle of the swing.
How the exam asks it. Expect at least one full chain problem. Expect ANDS and the turning error. The trap is adding east variation.

The arithmetic is the same arithmetic you've been doing since chapter 5, with a clock. Time is distance divided by groundspeed. Distance is groundspeed times time. Fuel is time times burn. Do it in hours and convert, or do it in minutes and keep a 60 in the right place. 26.2 miles at 92 knots is 26.2 divided by 92, times 60, which is 17.1 minutes.

The fuel rule is 91.151, and it's a floor. You can't begin a flight in an airplane under VFR unless, considering the wind and forecast weather, you have enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, at normal cruising speed, fly for 30 more minutes by day or 45 at night. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say anything about the whole trip, only to the first landing. It doesn't say anything about a diversion, except that the wind and weather you knew about count. And it doesn't say 30 minutes is enough. It says less than that is illegal.

The club plans Biscuit at 105 knots true at 7,500 feet and 8.0 gallons an hour. Those are planning numbers, a little pessimistic on purpose. To each departure add a gallon for start, taxi, and runup and a gallon for the climb, because she burns more climbing and goes slower over the ground doing it. The PHAK says plan for startup, taxi, and the higher burn in the climb, and then add reserve on top. My rule, and the club's, is that you land with an hour. That's 8 gallons. Legal is 4.

Two more preflight requirements. 91.103 says that before a flight that isn't in the vicinity of an airport you have to become familiar with the weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, the alternatives available if you can't finish the planned flight, and any known traffic delays. For any flight, the runway lengths at the airports you'll use and the takeoff and landing distance data. Alternatives is the word I want you to underline. And the clock: weather comes in Zulu, flight plans go in Zulu, and you live in Mountain Standard Time now, UTC minus 7. Your 8:40 departure is 1540Z.
How the exam asks it. Day 30, night 45, to the first point of intended landing. Calculation questions give you a groundspeed and burn and ask for fuel with reserve.

91.159 is the hemispheric rule. In level cruise more than 3,000 feet above the surface, VFR, below 18,000: on a magnetic course from 0 through 179, fly an odd thousand plus 500, like 7,500 or 9,500. On a magnetic course from 180 through 359, an even thousand plus 500, like 6,500 or 8,500. Magnetic course, not heading. The rule exists so eastbound and westbound traffic at the same altitude are a thousand feet apart.

Read the first clause again. More than 3,000 feet above the surface. Around here the ground is about 5,000 to 5,500 feet, and the Class B floors sit at 7,000 and 8,000. Under the shelves you're usually less than 3,000 AGL, and the rule doesn't apply. You still pick a sensible number, and out of habit I like the right one for your direction when the floors allow it. But on the test and in the airplane, the floors win, because a Class B clearance is a regulation too and the hemispheric rule has a door built into it.

Our shelves, from the FAA's own description. The Denver Class B is built out from a center point just south of the airport, in rings at 10, 15, 20, and 30 miles, cut into pie slices by radials and, in places, by roads. Over Centennial and the plains southeast, the floor is 8,000. Northeast of it, between 10 and 15 miles, a slice comes down to 7,000. Farther out, between 20 and 30 miles east, it lifts to 10,000. North, between 20 and 30, it's 8,000. Past 30 miles, there's nothing. Inside 10 miles a lot of it goes to the ground, and the rest starts low. My rule doesn't change: 300 feet below any floor unless a controller says the words cleared into the Bravo. Under 8,000, that's 7,700. Under 7,000, it's 6,700.

The Space Port is the interesting one. It's inside the 10 mile ring, but it sits in a notch, south of a line running east from the center and east of a county road, Imboden, that the FAA uses as a boundary, where the floor is 7,000 instead of the ground. North of that line, inside 10 miles, the Bravo goes to the surface. So you don't come into the Space Port from the north. You come in from the east, under the 7,000, and you leave to the south or east the same way.
And since someone always asks: a 172N runs out of climb somewhere around 14,000 feet on a good day, and you're not going to find out which day.
How the exam asks it. Hemispheric altitudes go by magnetic course and only apply above 3,000 ft AGL. Know which number is odd plus 500.

The VOR is a radio station on the ground that sends out a signal you can turn into a direction. It works line of sight, so the higher you are the farther you'll pick it up. It's going away slowly. The FAA is shutting down VORs it doesn't need, and the Denver VOR is on that list; this year they even rewrote the Class B's description so its center is a point on the map instead of that station. The test still asks about VORs, Biscuit still has one, and on a day the GPS quits you'll be glad.

A radial is a magnetic bearing from the station. The 030 radial is the line running out from the station toward the northeast, 030 degrees magnetic. On Biscuit's indicator you turn the OBS, the knob, to pick a course. The needle shows whether that course is left or right of you, and the TO or FROM flag says whether flying that course takes you toward the station or away from it. Centered needle, 030 under the index, FROM flag: you're on the 030 radial, northeast of the station. Same needle, same 030, TO flag: you're on the 210 radial, southwest of it, and flying 030 takes you to it. The indicator doesn't care which way the airplane is pointed. Set the course you want to fly and the needle reads the right way. Set the reciprocal and you get reverse sensing, where chasing the needle drives you away from it.

Identify it every time. The AIM says the only positive way to identify a VOR is its Morse code identifier or its recorded voice identifier, and not a controller saying its name. DEN is dash dot dot, dot, dash dot. During maintenance a station may send T E S T or nothing at all, and then you don't use it.

Accuracy is excellent, generally within a degree. The IFR check rules are worth knowing for the test: a ground check within plus or minus 4 degrees, an airborne check within plus or minus 6, and with two receivers on the same station, no more than 4 degrees apart. A degree off the radial is about a mile wide at 60 miles out and half a mile at 30. And the time-distance trick: turn so the station is off your wingtip, time how long it takes the bearing to change 10 degrees, and the seconds divided by the degrees give you minutes to the station. Ninety seconds for 10 degrees is nine minutes.
How the exam asks it. Radial means from. The indicator ignores heading. Morse code is the positive ID. Expect a time-to-station calculation.

The panel GPS is the best navigation tool you'll ever have in this airplane, and the AIM and the PHAK both want you to treat it as one tool among several. The AIM says VFR pilots should integrate GPS with other electronic navigation when they can, and with pilotage and dead reckoning. That's the sentence the checkride examiner will ask you to explain.

Here's why. A VFR panel unit or a handheld has no RAIM alerting. RAIM is the receiver checking itself, making sure it has enough good satellites to trust its own answer. Without it, the box can lose satellites or work out a bad position and not tell you. The fix is a cross-check. If the GPS and the interstate disagree, believe the interstate and find out why.

The database is the second thing. There's no legal requirement to keep a VFR database current, and the AIM recommends you do, and says not to use a moving map with an old database around critical airspace. Out here critical airspace means everything with a Bravo floor over it. Ours is current. Check the date on the start page anyway, because checking is the habit.

Third, the head-down problem. The PHAK says if you're going to use your own waypoints, enter them before you take off, and don't build routes in flight. Know the buttons on the ground. Every minute your eyes are in the box is a minute nobody's looking for the Bonanza.
How the exam asks it. Know what RAIM does and that most VFR receivers lack the alert. The safe answer is always a cross-check.

You've used it. Now the fine print. The AIM calls it radar traffic information service: the controller tells you about radar targets that might come close enough to your route to deserve your attention. It's provided when the controller thinks they can, which depends on radar limits, traffic, workload, and how busy the frequency is, and the AIM says their reason for saying no isn't subject to question. In practice around Denver they almost always say yes.

What it isn't. It doesn't relieve you of seeing and avoiding other airplanes. It doesn't include vectors away from traffic unless you ask. It isn't a Class B clearance, and radar contact isn't permission to climb. And while you have it, you monitor that frequency all the time, because if you go silent the controller has to wonder whether you've lost your radio or worse. When you don't want it anymore, tell them before you change frequencies, and go back to 1200 unless they've done it for you.

The request is the same five things you've practiced: who you are, where you are, your altitude, what you want, and where you're going. At Greeley there's no tower, so near the airport Approach will terminate radar service and you'll switch to the airport's common frequency. You talk to the airplanes yourself there.
How the exam asks it. Flight following is workload permitting and never relieves you of see and avoid. That's most of what the test asks.

A VFR flight plan is your search and rescue insurance. Inside the continental U.S. it's not normally required. The AIM strongly recommends one anyway. You file it with Flight Service, you open it yourself after takeoff, and you close it yourself when you're down. Towers don't open VFR flight plans and they don't close them, because they don't know who's on one. If you don't close it, or update it, within half an hour after your ETA, search and rescue starts. People will get in cars. They'll call your mother.

91.153 lists what goes in it: your aircraft identification, the type, your name and address, departure point and proposed time, the route, cruising altitude, true airspeed, your first intended landing and the estimated time to get there, fuel on board in hours, the number of people aboard, and anything else ATC needs. The AIM says filing is now done on the international form, FAA Form 7233-4, and the apps fill it in for you.

For a trip with stops, file a separate flight plan for each leg. That's straight out of the AIM. A proposal is kept for about two hours after your proposed departure time, so if you're late by more than that, file again. You can activate one with an assumed departure time, but the AIM warns that if you don't update it, search and rescue will run off that time. Easier to just open it on the radio after takeoff and close it on the phone after you shut down.

One more item the ACS lists under cross-country planning: interception. If a military aircraft ever pulls up next to you, follow its instructions and read AIM chapter 5, section 6 before then. It won't happen to you over Greeley. Know where it lives anyway.
How the exam asks it. Thirty minutes after ETA is the search and rescue trigger. Fuel on a flight plan goes in hours, not gallons.

Getting lost isn't the emergency. Staying lost while the fuel goes down is. The PHAK's first step, if you can't see a town, is to climb, minding traffic and weather, because altitude lets you see farther, pick up navigation signals farther, and show up on radar farther. Under our shelves you can't climb much, so the shelf is part of the answer too: you know you're under something, and that narrows it down.

Then look for the big stuff. An interstate. A railroad running next to it. A reservoir. The name on a water tower if you're low enough, which you shouldn't need to be. Tune and identify a VOR and find what radial you're on; two radials from two stations cross at your position. If you have GPS and it's working, use it, and cross-check it.

And talk. Approach can find you on radar and give you vectors. Flight Service and some facilities can find you by direction finding, where they ask you to hold the transmit button for a few seconds. If it's getting serious, say so, declare it, and squawk 7700. The common mnemonic is climb, communicate, confess, comply. The confess part is the hard one for people like you. Do it early. Controllers have heard worse.
How the exam asks it. Climb first, then use every resource. Lost procedure questions reward asking for help early.

A diversion is when you decide not to go where you planned. The PHAK lists the reasons: unpredicted weather, a malfunction, or poor planning, which we're going to avoid. It says risk management becomes the priority, and it names the case you'll meet most: a pre-planned or in-flight diversion around hazardous weather. Before any cross-country, look along the route for airports and places to land, and for navigation aids you could use.

In the air, take shortcuts. You don't plot on a chart in a bumpy cockpit. Pick the alternate, estimate the course from the chart or a VOR rose, and if there's time, start the turn over something you can recognize, so you know exactly where the new leg began. In a real emergency, turn first and figure later. Then note the time, use the nearest winds to work a heading and a groundspeed, and from those an arrival time and the fuel it costs. Fly the airplane while you do it.

For small corrections there's the 60 to 1 rule. One degree off course is about one mile off for every 60 miles flown. If you're 1 mile off after 10 miles, your heading was off 6 degrees. Turn 6 to stop the drift, plus enough to get back by the next checkpoint: 1 mile in 16 more is about 4 degrees. Ten degrees total, then back to 6 once you're on the line.

Now the weather you'll actually see. In November the big July thunderstorms are gone. What we get instead behind a cold front is cold air with a little instability in it, and that builds snow showers over the plains. Small ones, sometimes only a few miles across, with flat dark bases and a gray curtain under them, and virga, snow that evaporates before it reaches the ground, hanging off the edges. They look soft. Inside one the visibility goes to nothing in about a second and the ground disappears, which for a VFR pilot is the whole emergency. You don't go under them, through them, or close to them. You give them miles, and you go around the side that has clear air and a way home.
The days are short now too. Sunset's around half past four. Plan to be tied down with daylight left over.
How the exam asks it. For diversion questions: turn promptly toward the alternate, then compute. For off-course questions, use the 60 to 1 rule.

Thursday, November 12, four in the afternoon, the briefing room. Jordan had come off a shift at seven that morning and slept until two, and she still had the station's coffee taste in her mouth. Abby had the Denver sectional unfolded across both tables with a coffee mug on each corner, the way you'd pin down a patient who didn't want an IV.

Jordan laid the new plotter from the little airport symbol at Centennial to the one east of Greeley and ran a pencil down the edge. Fifty three miles. It went north, a little east, and straight through the solid blue rings around Denver International. Not near them. Through the middle of the innermost one, where the number in the blue said the Bravo came all the way down to the ground.
Pretty line, Abby said. Your trip. Where does it go?
A. Bend it east around the inner rings, and write the floor of every shelf she'll pass under.
B. Go around the west side instead, past downtown and Rocky Mountain Metro, under the western shelves.
C. Keep the straight line and fly it low, at about 6,000 feet, so she stays under all of the shelves.
D. Keep the straight line, and ask Denver Approach for a Bravo clearance when she gets close to the rings.

She erases the line and draws it again in pieces. East first, out over the Aurora Reservoir, then a turn northeast to Strasburg on I-70, then due north across open country to Roggen on I-76, then northwest into Greeley. Seventy two miles instead of fifty three. Next to each piece she writes the floor in a column, the way she'd write vitals: 80, 80, then 70 for a stretch, 80, 100, 80, nothing. Abby taps the 70 with her pencil. That's the one people miss. Everybody knows Centennial's 80. Nobody looks up out there. She checks the turn east of the reservoir. There's nothing on the ground at that corner, so make it a GPS point. Build it Sunday morning at the kitchen table, not on the climbout. Jordan writes BEND next to it. Abby considers this. Fine. It's a bend.

That's it. Route planning starts with airspace (PA.I.D.K1). Going around the inner rings keeps the flight under the shelves without needing a clearance, and listing every floor along the route is how you avoid the one that drops lower than you expect.
That evening she took the nav log to Claire's, because Claire had texted tamales, come eat them or I'll cry, and because Ellie had math homework and wanted company.

Ellie's homework was angles. Jordan's homework was angles. They sat across from each other at the kitchen table with the overhead light on, and after twenty minutes Ellie looked up from a protractor and asked where north was.
Jordan pointed out the window, at the Johnsons' garage. Ellie produced a little plastic compass from a cereal box and set it on the table. The needle settled a bit to the right of the garage.

Your north and my north are different. Mine's the map's. Yours is the magnet's. Around here they're about seven degrees apart. So who's right? Both of us. You just have to know how far apart. Ellie found that unsatisfying and said so.

Biscuit's compass card, taped under the compass. FOR   N    30   60   E    120  150 STEER 001  031  062  092  121  150 FOR   S    210  240  W    300  330 STEER 178  208  238  268  299  330 RADIOS ON. SWUNG 3/14/24, M. TRAN

The first row of her log: Centennial to BEND, true course 079 off the plotter. Wind at 9,000 forecast from 320 true at 16 knots. Her wind correction angle came out 8 degrees left, which made the true heading 071. Variation 7 east. Ellie watched her pencil hover.
A. Skip the conversion. The GPS will draw the course line, and she can fly whatever keeps it centered.
B. Subtract the 7 from the 079 course for 072, and put the wind correction in later, in flight.
C. Subtract the 7 east from the true heading: 064 magnetic.
D. Add the 7 east to the true heading: 078 magnetic, since easterly variation turns the number up.

MH 064. She says it the way Abby does, East is least, and Ellie says West is best right back without being asked, which means somebody taught her, and Jordan doesn't have to ask who. Then the card. 064 is closest to 060, which says steer 062: two more. CH 066. Ellie leans over the card and reads it upside down. So the airplane has its own north too? Sort of. Two degrees off. Because it's old? Because it's full of wires and an engine. Ellie decides this is Biscuit's fault and not Jordan's, which is generous of her, and goes back to her protractor.

Yep. That's the one. PHAK chapter 16: TC WCA TH V MH D CH. East variation is subtracted, so a true heading of 071 with 7° E is a magnetic heading of 064. Deviation from the card then gives the compass heading.

Monday, November 16. She'd flown the practice area alone that morning, 1.2 on the Hobbs, her first time out of sight of the tower by herself, and had spent most of it looking at the ground and saying the names of things out loud. Now it was the kitchen table and the altitude column.

Kneeboard, leg one, the floors. KAPA TO BEND: B 80. NOTHING ABOVE 7,700.. BEND TO STRASBURG: B 80.. STRASBURG TO ROGGEN: 80 FOR 3 MI. THEN 70 FOR ABOUT 7. THEN 80. THEN 100. THEN 80 AGAIN AT THE INTERSTATE.. ROGGEN TO KGXY: 80 FOR ABOUT 10. THEN NOTHING.. GROUND: ABOUT 5,000 TO 5,500 UNDER ALL OF IT. KGXY FIELD 4,697.

The Strasburg to Roggen leg was the long one, 26 miles due north across country with no towns to speak of, and its magnetic course was 351. Westbound. She knew the rule for westbound. She also knew the column.
A. 8,500. A 351 magnetic course is westbound, and westbound is an even thousand plus 500.
B. 7,500, down to 6,700 under the 70, then back up. Below 3,000 feet above the ground the rule doesn't apply.
C. 6,500 for the whole leg. It's under every floor on the column, so there's nothing to keep track of.
D. 7,500 for the whole leg. It's under 8,000, which is the number for everything out east.

She works it: 7,500 over ground at about 5,400 near Strasburg is 2,100 feet above it, under 3,000, so 91.159 doesn't apply, and she picks her numbers by the shelves. 6,700 is 300 under the 70. She draws a small step down in the altitude column at 3 miles and a step up at 10. Abby reads it that night and sends back one line. Good. Past Greeley, if you're ever above 3,000 AGL westbound, it's 8,500. Not today.

Exactly right. 91.159 applies in level cruise more than 3,000 feet above the surface. Under the Denver shelves the terrain puts her below that, so the Class B floors set the altitude, with Abby's 300 foot margin below each one.

Thursday, November 19, the dual cross-country, Abby in the right seat with a thermos and a pack of yellow sticky notes. They flew the whole route the way Jordan had planned it: BEND, Strasburg, the step down under the 70, and for twenty minutes it was very calm and very flat.

Somewhere north of I-70 Abby said Hood, and Jordan put the foggles on, and for five minutes she flew whatever Abby said. Left turns. A climb. A long right turn. A descent. She lost count of the turns on purpose because Abby told her to.
I have the airplane. Hood off. When Jordan looked up, there was a sticky note over the GPS screen with a face drawn on it, a frown. GPS just died. You're lost. Your airplane.
Below: fields, brown and white, a dirt road, a center pivot like a long metal arm laid out in a circle. 6,600 on the altimeter. Nothing she recognized.
A. Hold the heading, find a big landmark, and match it on the chart with a VOR radial.
B. Descend low enough to read a name off the nearest water tower, and head toward it.
C. Peel off the sticky note. On a real flight the GPS is the first thing she'd look at.
D. Call Denver Approach and ask where she is, before trying anything on her own.

She rolls wings level on 360 and holds it, the PHAK's line running in her head. Ahead, maybe five miles, a straight gray line angles across her path toward the east-northeast with a thinner line beside it, an interstate and a railroad running together, which on this chart can only be I-76. She tunes the Denver VOR and listens: dash dot dot, dot, dash dot. Turns the OBS until the needle centers with a FROM flag. 028. She finds the 028 radial on the chart, follows it out from the station to where it crosses south of I-76. About twenty miles northeast of the Denver VOR, south of the interstate. Roggen's just ahead, where we'll meet the interstate. Abby peels off the sticky note. The GPS agrees within a mile. Abby writes something on her kneeboard and doesn't say what.

That's it. PHAK lost procedures: hold the heading, use prominent features, and fix your position with VOR radials or GPS, then communicate if needed. Identifying the VOR by Morse code is the AIM's positive identification.

Twelve miles southeast of Greeley, Approach let them go. Radar service terminated, squawk VFR, frequency change approved. Jordan switched to Greeley's common frequency and listened, and nobody said anything for a long time, which at Centennial never happened.

The AWOS said wind calm, visibility 10, few clouds at 12,000, altimeter three zero two one. On her kneeboard she'd copied two lines from the Chart Supplement the night before: RWY 35 PREFERRED WHEN WIND LESS THAN 5 KTS. OIL DRILLING RIGS UP TO 120 FT ON AND INVOF ARPT. And the pattern altitude, 5,500 rounded, 800 feet above the field.
Greeley was spread across the windshield, the city on the left and the airport on its east side, two long runways in an L. Abby sat with her hands in her lap.
A. Fly straight in to runway 28, the closest one. Nobody's talking, so nobody's there.
B. Announce at ten miles, cross over to the west side well above the pattern, and enter on the 45 for left downwind 35.
C. Announce on the frequency and fly a straight-in to 35, since it's calm and she's south anyway.
D. Join the downwind for 35 at 6,500, a thousand feet above pattern altitude, so she's above anybody there.

Greeley traffic, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, ten miles southeast, inbound for left traffic runway three five, Greeley. She crosses the field at 6,500, well above anything in the pattern, flies out to the west, descends to 5,500 away from the downwind, and turns back in on a 45. A Skyhawk comes up on the frequency, already on downwind. She sees it, calls it, follows it. Base, final, ten thousand feet of runway in front of her. Abby, as the mains touch: You could land three times on this one. Don't.

Yep. That's the one. At nontowered airports the standard entry is the 45 to the downwind at pattern altitude, with position reports on the common frequency. Crossing well above the pattern and descending outside it keeps you clear of traffic already there.
Decision six. One leg at a time.

Saturday, November 21, 8 PM. She'd worked Friday into Saturday, a quiet one for once, and slept until two. Now the kitchen table again, with the finished log, a mug of tea gone cold, and the chart folded to the Denver panel so the route ran up the middle of the fold.

Nav log, N4791E, Sunday 11/22. TAS 105. Wind 320/16 (FB 9000). Var 7E. Dev from nearest card heading.. LEG 1. KAPA TO KGXY. CHECKPOINT   TC  WCA TH  MH  DEV CH   DIST GS  ETE FUEL ALT BEND RES.)  079 -8  071 064 +2  066 16.4 112 9   1.2  7500 TOTAL 72.4 NM, 46 MIN. CRUISE 6.1 TAXI 1.0 CLIMB 1.0 8.1 GAL. LEG 2. KGXY TO KCFO. 6500 (B 70). TOTAL 55.5 NM, 29 MIN. CRUISE 3.9 2.0 5.9 GAL. PLAN B: EAST AROUND ANYTHING THAT BUILDS. NEVER WEST (BRAVO). OR BACK TO KGXY.. LEG 3. KCFO TO KAPA. B 70 TOTAL 26.4 NM, 15 MIN. CRUISE 2.1 2.0 4.1 GAL. DAY: 154.3 NM FLOWN, 111.8 POINT TO POINT. FUEL 18.1 GAL. LAND WITH AN HOUR (8.0).

Flight plan, leg one, the way the app laid it out. AIRCRAFT: N4791E. C172.. PILOT: JORDAN E. REYES, AURORA CO.. DEPARTURE: KAPA, 1540Z.. ROUTE: BEND (USER WAYPOINT 39 37.2N 104 30.0W), STRASBURG, ROGGEN.. CRUISING ALTITUDE: 7,500 (6,700 NORTH OF STRASBURG UNDER CLASS B 7,000). TRUE AIRSPEED: 105 KTS.. DESTINATION: KGXY. ESTIMATED TIME EN ROUTE: 0 HR 53 MIN.. FUEL ON BOARD: 3 HR MIN.. PERSONS ON BOARD: 1. AIRCRAFT COLOR: WHITE, MAROON STRIPE.. REMARKS: STUDENT PILOT. SOLO CROSS-COUNTRY.
The app had a button at the bottom that said FILE. She'd filled it in twice to be sure. Under it, smaller, another one: ADD STOP.
A. Skip the flight plans. She'll be on flight following the whole way, and that's ATC watching her anyway.
B. File one plan for the whole day, with the stops in the remarks, and let the tower close it when she's home.
C. File one per leg with assumed departure times, so each opens on its own and she can skip the radio.
D. File one per leg, open each with Flight Service after takeoff, and close it once she's down.

Three plans, three ETAs. She writes the closing times on her kneeboard in red, under each leg, with the half hour added: CLOSE BY 1003. CLOSE BY 1110. CLOSE BY 1230. Then she texts Abby the times, because Abby says to tell somebody too and Abby is somebody. Abby: close every one. I'll know. Then: BEND is a good name.

Exactly right. The AIM recommends a separate VFR flight plan for each leg of a stopover flight, activated by the pilot after departure and closed by the pilot after landing. Search and rescue begins if a plan isn't closed within 30 minutes of ETA.

Sunday, November 22, 6:40 in the morning, the briefing room, still dark outside. Abby had come in on a Sunday to review the planning, which 61.93 said she had to, and she'd brought two breakfast burritos from the place on Arapahoe Road, which nothing said she had to. She pushed one across the table without comment.

Weather, printed at 6:32 AM. METAR KAPA 221253Z 32006KT 10SM FEW120 M04/M12 A3016 RMK AO2. TAF KAPA 221120Z 2212/2312 32008KT P6SM FEW120.      FM221800 34008KT P6SM SCT025.      PROB30 2221/2224 4SM -SHSN BKN060.      FM230100 34006KT P6SM SKC. FB DATA BASED ON 220600Z, VALID 221200Z, FOR USE 0900-1800Z. FT   3000   6000   9000    12000   18000 DEN               3216-06 3022-12 2934-24 GFA, PLAINS E AND NE OF DENVER: ISOLD -SHSN DEVELOPING AFT 17Z. BASES 8000-9000 MSL. VIS 1-3SM IN SHSN.

She did the times out loud. Twenty one hundred Zulu, minus seven: two in the afternoon. Seventeen Zulu: ten in the morning. The TAF only covered five miles around Centennial. The graphical forecast covered the space in between, which was where she'd actually be.

Her card was above the mag switch. On Monday, at the kitchen table, with Abby on speaker, she'd added a line at the bottom for cross-countries: CEILING 5,000 AGL, VIS 10, AND A WAY OUT ON EVERY LEG. Abby finished her burrito. Tell me the plan. Then tell me what turns you around.
A. Cancel. There are snow showers in the forecast, and she doesn't want to meet one alone.
B. Go, and decide about showers if she sees any. The TAF doesn't have them until two at the earliest.
C. Go now instead, wheels up by 7:00, right around sunrise, and be home before anything builds.
D. Go at 8:40, home by 1:00, east around anything that builds, or back to Greeley if east isn't open.

She lays it out in order, the way she'd hand off a patient. Departure 8:40, Greeley by 9:35, fuel and close and file, out by 10:05, Space Port by 10:40, home by noon. One o'clock is the line. A shower on any leg: east around it, at least five miles, because west of the route is the Bravo. If east isn't open, back to Greeley and wait. Abby listens to all of it, nodding at nothing, and then uncaps the green pen and writes the second endorsement in her logbook, slowly, the way she never writes anything. Known conditions. That's the phrase in the reg. You just told me what they are.

That's it. 61.93(d) requires the instructor to review current and forecast weather and determine the flight can be completed under VFR. A planned finish time with margin, a defined turn-back point, and a pre-planned diversion are what the PHAK calls managing weather risk before the flight.
The club chat from the night before was still open on her phone.
A message from Russ Kim. biscuit's back from the burger run. 26 by the stick, 13 a side, so 24 usable. self serve card reader at APA is down again, sorry, not my fault, i blame the reader
A message from Marisol Tran. Truck can come Sunday, there's a callout fee. Greeley has fuel. Jordan, the selector's sticking short of BOTH again. Lift and twist, feel for the click, don't force it.

7:35 AM. Minus four on the ramp and the sky clean and pale over the plains. Walt was at the tie down, which on a Sunday morning surprised her until she remembered he'd been a dispatcher for thirty years and probably hadn't slept in on a weekend since the eighties. He had a coffee in each hand and gave her one. She dipped both tanks with the clear tube. Thirteen and thirteen, near enough. Twenty four usable.
Walt looked at her nav log over his glasses. Every release I ever signed had one number on it I cared about more than the others. What do you land with?
A. Fly leg one on 24, then top off at Greeley, so every landing comes with at least an hour.
B. Leave on 24, and decide about fuel at Greeley after she sees what the gauges say.
C. Skip fuel all day. 24 usable covers every leg and still leaves more than the 30 minutes 91.151 asks for.
D. Go with Russ's 24 from the chat and skip the dipstick. Russ is careful about fuel.

Leg one is 8.1. I land at Greeley with about 16, two hours. I top off there and land everywhere after that with two or more. Walt nods slowly. And if Greeley's pump is down too? She hadn't thought of that. Then I have 16 at Greeley, and the rest of the day needs 10 plus my hour. I'd wait or call the truck. I wouldn't leave. That's an alternate, he says. Most students think an alternate is a place. It's a decision you made before you needed it.

Yep. That's the one. Planning fuel at every stop, with a reserve well above the 91.151 minimum and a backup if fuel isn't available, follows the PHAK's guidance to add an adequate reserve and the ACS's fuel planning risk element.
8:12 AM. A text from her mother.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Where today.
A text from Jordan Reyes. Greeley, then a stop near Watkins, then home. About three hours.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Text me when you're down. Each time.
In the flight bag, next to the green notebook, her logbook lay open to the new page.

Jordan's logbook, endorsements. 11/19/26. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has received the required solo cross-country training. I find they have met the applicable requirements of 14 CFR 61.93 and are proficient to make solo cross-country flights in a Cessna 172N aircraft, airplane single-engine.. Limitations: Day VFR only. Ceiling 5,000 AGL or higher and visibility 10 SM or better at departure, destination, and en route reporting points. Remain at least 5 SM from any precipitation. Surface wind 10 knots or less, gusts no more than 5 over, crosswind component 5 knots or less. FLIGHT FOLLOWING ON EVERY LEG. No Class B. On the ground at KAPA by 1300 local.. /s/ 11/19/26 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027. 11/22/26. I have reviewed the cross-country planning of Jordan E. Reyes. I find the planning and preparation to be correct to make the solo flight from KAPA to KAPA via BEND, Strasburg, and Roggen with landings at KGXY and KCFO in a Cessna 172N aircraft on 11/22/26. Limitations of the 11/19/26 endorsement apply and are met.. /s/ 11/22/26 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027
The capitals weren't for her, Abby had said, they were for the endorsement. Jordan had decided to believe that.

Runup on Alpha near the end of 35R, the left door latched top and bottom, both of them touched. Mags, carb heat, the selector lifted and twisted to BOTH until it clicked. Centennial Ground, Niner One Echo, ready for departure, runway three five right. Niner One Echo, monitor tower. Then tower, and the takeoff, wind three two zero at six, right turn eastbound approved, the door holding, the reservoir coming up blue and flat on the left of the nose, and then the tower: Niner One Echo, frequency change approved.
A. Ask tower to set up flight following for her, and stay with tower until they hand her to Approach.
B. Wait until she's past the reservoir, where it's quieter, and then decide if she needs it.
C. Call Denver Approach right away: who she is, where, her altitude, and flight following to Greeley.
D. Get the squawk code, then turn the volume down so she can concentrate. The code keeps her on radar.

Denver Approach, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, four miles east of Centennial, climbing through seven thousand for seven thousand five hundred, request flight following to Greeley. A man's voice gives her a code. She reads it back and dials it in, and he says Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, radar contact, four miles east of Centennial, maintain VFR at or below seven thousand five hundred. Level at 7,500 she asks him for a minute off the frequency, opens the flight plan with Flight Service, and comes back, and BEND comes up on the GPS where she put it at the kitchen table, and the reservoir slides under the nose right on time.

Exactly right. AIM 4-1-15: radar traffic advisories are available to VFR pilots on request. The request gives who, where, altitude, and destination. Opening the VFR flight plan after takeoff starts the search and rescue clock at the real departure time.

8:57, Strasburg, right on time: the interstate, the grain elevator, the little grid of streets, and she turned north onto 347 and wrote the time on the log. Three miles later she stepped down to 6,700 for the 70.

9:04. By the log she should have been ten miles past Strasburg at 9:03 and a half. She checked her position against a section road crossing she'd marked, and then against the GPS, which agreed with the road: ten miles north of Strasburg, a mile left of the line. West. Toward Denver, where to her left, fifteen miles off, the white peaks of the airport's tent roof sat on the horizon like something left out to dry.
She looked at the heading indicator, then the compass. The gyro said 347. The compass, after it stopped swinging, said 343.
A. Center the GPS needle and fly whatever heading keeps it there. She can fix the log at Roggen.
B. Turn six degrees right to stop the drift, and fly the rest of the way parallel, a mile left.
C. Reset the gyro, correct back onto the line by Roggen, and work a new ETA from the real groundspeed.
D. Hold her heading. I-76 and Roggen will show up in a few minutes, and she can sort it out then.

Gyro first: wings level, speed steady, the middle of the compass swing, 343. She resets it. So she'd been flying 343 the whole time, four degrees left of the plan, and that's most of the mile. The rest is wind. One mile off in ten is six degrees of track error: four from the gyro, two from the wind. So the heading that holds the line is 349. One mile back in sixteen is about four more. She turns to 353 on the newly honest gyro and watches the GPS needle start to walk back toward center. Ten miles in seven minutes is 86 knots, not 92: more headwind than the forecast. Sixteen miles at 86 is 11.3 minutes. ROGGEN 0915. At 9:15 the needle touches center and the interstate and the railroad come out from under the nose together, and she says Roggen to nobody.

That's it. The heading indicator drifts and must be reset to the compass. The 60 to 1 rule turns the mile into degrees: 6 degrees of track error to take out, plus about 4 to get back on the line by the next checkpoint. A groundspeed from actual time and distance gives the corrected ETA.

Greeley went by the way it was supposed to. A left downwind for 35 behind nobody, a landing she was proud of, the fuel pit, the flight plan closed and the next one filed, a text to her mother: Down at Greeley. Her mother: Ok. She was off again at 10:05 with Approach giving her a new code, southeast at 7,500 toward Roggen, the low sun just right of the nose.

She saw it from fifteen miles out and didn't understand it at first. Ahead, a little left of the nose, a piece of the sky had gone gray. A flat dark base, maybe eight thousand feet, and under it a soft curtain reaching all the way to the fields, with lighter streamers hanging off its edges that didn't reach anything. It hadn't been there at Greeley. By Roggen, 10:17, it was right on her line to Strasburg, about twelve miles ahead, a few miles across, drifting southeast the way the winds aloft said it would. Slow.
To its left, west, the sky was clear all the way to the tent roof and the shelves. To its right, east, clear and bright over empty country all the way to I-70. Behind her Greeley sat in sunshine.
A. Go around the west side. It's the short side, and the Space Port is west of the line anyway.
B. Drop to 6,500 and slide under the edge of it. It's light snow, and she can see through it.
C. Turn back to Greeley, land, and wait for it to blow through.
D. Hold 138 past Roggen to leave it a wide berth on the east side, tell Approach, then turn for Strasburg.

She doesn't turn at Roggen. She notes the time, 10:17, and keeps the heading she has, 138, which runs southeast down the clear side. Denver Approach, Niner One Echo, deviating east for a snow shower, then direct Strasburg. Niner One Echo, roger, no traffic observed in that direction. On the kneeboard: 19 miles to a point ten miles east of her line, out ahead of the shower because it's drifting toward her return leg, 121 knots, nine and a half minutes. Then a true course of 223 to Strasburg, 14.8 miles, which the crab and the variation bring back to 223 on the compass, 106 knots, eight and a half minutes. STRASBURG 1035. Four and a half minutes longer than the plan, and six tenths of a gallon. At 10:26 she turns. The shower slides by on her right, close enough to see the snow inside it moving, the streamers of virga glowing white where the sun gets under them, and then it's behind her and I-70 is ahead, and Strasburg is exactly where she left it.

Yep. That's the one. The PHAK describes a pre-planned diversion around hazardous weather: start at a recognizable point, note the time, compute heading, groundspeed, ETA, and fuel, and fly the airplane. East had clear air and higher Class B floors. The drift was toward her return leg, which is why the turn point went wide enough to keep her about five miles from the edge.

Strasburg, then west down the interstate toward the Space Port with the ATIS in her ear: wind three three zero at eight, visibility one zero, few clouds at two thousand five hundred, landing runway three five. She was under the 80. She called the tower from eight miles east, then stepped down to 6,500 as she passed under the 70.
Cessna Niner One Echo, Space Port Tower, enter right downwind runway three five, report midfield.

On the downwind, with the long runway off her right wing, the tower came back. Niner One Echo, extend downwind, number two following a Citation on a four mile final. Caution wake turbulence. She found it, a small white jet low on final, gear down, catching the sun. She called it in sight. It looked harmless from there. Abby had told her what they all look like from there.
A. Extend downwind for extra spacing, then fly a normal approach and land on the numbers as usual.
B. Stay at or above the Citation's glidepath, note where it touches down, and land past that spot.
C. Turn base right behind it to keep the spacing tight, so tower doesn't have to hold anybody else up.
D. Fly a lower, flatter approach under its path, so she can touch down short of where it landed.

The tower calls her base. She turns final a little high on purpose and keeps the picture steep, above where the jet came down, and watches for its touchdown: a puff off the mains about a thousand feet down the runway. She aims for a spot well past it, which on 8,000 feet of runway costs her nothing at all. Her wheels touch beyond the puff. The Citation is already turning off ahead of her, small and white and harmless, and she lets out a breath she'd been keeping since the downwind.

Exactly right. AIM 7-4-6: when landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway, stay at or above its final approach flight path, note its touchdown point, and land beyond it. Wake vortices sink and trail behind and below the aircraft that made them.
She was on the ground at the Space Port at 10:43, which was three minutes later than the log, and she taxied to the FBO behind a lineman with orange wands who waved her in like she was a 737.

Mixture, mags, master. The propeller stopped. She sat with her hands in her lap the way she had after the discovery flight in April, and then she did the things in order. She called Flight Service and closed the plan. She texted her mother: Down at the Space Port. Her mother: What is a space port. Watkins. Text me from home.
Then she dipped the tanks out of habit and wrote the number on the log next to the time, in pencil, the way Walt wrote everything.

Inside, the FBO was warm and empty, a television on mute with the radar loop running and a vending machine that sold hot chocolate for a dollar fifty. She got one and sat in a leather chair by the window with Danny's headset on the seat next to her. On the screen, the little green blob that had been her shower drifted southeast past Byers and came apart. Home was clear. She had two hours before Abby's line and needed fifteen minutes of them. She stayed in the chair anyway.
Somewhere in the second half of the hot chocolate she noticed it.

Since 7:10 that morning, since Abby capped the green pen, she hadn't thought about him. Not at the runup. Not at BEND, or Strasburg, or the gyro that had drifted four degrees, or Greeley, where she'd stood at the fuel pit with his headset around her neck and the wind going through her coat. Not at the curtain. Three and a half hours. She'd had his headset on her head the entire time, and his E6B in the side pocket with his pencil dot on it, and she'd flown his airplane to Greeley, which was a place he'd flown, and she had not thought about Danny once.

It landed on her like forgetting a birthday. Like walking past the house of somebody whose funeral you went to and noticing you'd been humming. Eight months, and the first three free hours she'd had, she'd spent them without him and hadn't noticed until they were over. She put the cup down. She looked at the headset. She felt, for a minute, about as bad as she'd felt in March.
Then she put the headset on and went home.

The leg home was fifteen minutes and nothing happened in it. South from the Space Port under the 70, BEND coming up on the GPS where she'd built it, a right turn at BEND, the reservoir sliding by on the right, Centennial Tower giving her a right downwind for 35R and a landing she made without hurrying. She closed the third flight plan from the tie down at 11:58, chained Biscuit down tight, and texted her mother Home. Her mother sent back a heart, which she had never done before, and then, a minute later, as if to correct the record: Ok.
Claire texted while she was putting the cover on.
A text from Claire Reyes. El wants to know if Greeley smells. She says her dad told her it did.
A text from Jordan Reyes. Didn't notice. Had the vents closed. Tell her I'll ask.

She sat in the left seat with the door open and took out the green notebook. On Monday she'd found the page and folded the corner down without reading it, because she'd decided she'd read his first cross-country after she'd flown hers, and not before. It was July. Eleven years ago.

Danny's logbook, a page from July, eleven years ago. July 18. FIRST SOLO XC!!! C152 52B from the school. KAPA, Greeley, Front Range, KAPA. 2.6 on the Hobbs. Planned 2.2. You can see where this is going.. Went around the east side like a good boy. Strasburg, fine. Then I got to the next interstate and followed it, and it turns out you're supposed to cross that one, because it goes to Nebraska. Climbed. Read a water tower: WIGGINS. Wiggins is not Greeley. Turned to the heading I should have been on in the first place, found the river, found Greeley by the smell. Feedlots. You could land on that smell.. Front Range tower lady said "Welcome to Front Range" like she meant it. Bought a Coke. Called nobody.. Here's the thing I want on the record. For two and a half hours I did not think about one other thing. Not work, not money, not the guy at the shop, not anything. Just the next checkpoint and the gas and the next checkpoint. Nobody tells you that's the best part. It's not the view. It's the quiet in your head.. Jordan thinks too much. She'd like this. She'd never admit it.
She read the last line again. Then the one before it.

The guilt from the FBO came back for a second when she got to the end, and then it went, the way a pager tone hangs in your ear after the pager's quiet. Two and a half hours of quiet in your head, he'd called it. He wrote that in July with a Coke from the Front Range FBO sweating on the page, you could see the ring, and he put her name under it. She'd gotten three and a half. He'd have been smug about that on her behalf. He'd have said she beat his time and got lost less, and she'd have said Wiggins wasn't even in the same county, and he'd have done the bark.
She didn't feel bad anymore. She sat a while longer in the cold cockpit and didn't think about much.

Then she took Danny's E6B out of the side pocket and looked at the wind side. His pencil dot, with the little circle around it. She'd worked every problem for two weeks around it, and she'd thought more than once about rubbing it out with her thumb. She put it back in the pocket the way it was.

Walt came out of the hangar as she was leaving, with the club fuel log on a clipboard and the Greeley receipt stapled to it. He looked at the fuel column, then at her. That's a column I'd have signed. He tucked the clipboard under his arm. Eight months. Four left. I'm starting to think I'll be wrong. Then, because he was Walt: Starting.
That night, at 9:22, the phone buzzed on the kitchen table next to the folded chart.

A text from Abby Strand. Saw the log. The deviation was textbook, I mean that literally, I'm putting it in my lesson notes. Next: night. Three hours, ten full stops, one cross-country over 100 miles. Then the long one, 150 and three stops, and you pick the route. Not Greeley. It smells.
